title: Speech rooted in the mind
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: a boy tells his teacher an awkward truth, and a chant asks words and mind to match
carry: satya: let your words match your mind
tomorrow: what's hidden behind a lid made of gold?

segments.voice: The peace chants, day six. Yesterday, apyayantu and the straw Agni couldn't burn: the power in your senses is Brahman's. Today, the mouth and the mind.

A boy named Satyakama wants to study the Veda, and a teacher will ask about his family line. So he asks his mother. She tells him the plain truth: she was young, working as a servant in many houses, and she doesn't know his line. Just say you're Satyakama, son of Jabala. So he does, word for word, to the teacher Gautama. And Gautama says: no one but a true brahmin could speak like that. You haven't strayed from the truth. Go fetch firewood. I'll teach you.
screen: `WHAT IS YOUR FAMILY LINE?` → `THE PLAIN TRUTH, WORD FOR WORD.` → `YOU HAVEN'T STRAYED FROM THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: That story is in the Chandogya, and it sits close to today's chant, the one tradition sets with the Aitareya Upanishad, known by its first words, van me manasi. In plain words: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind rooted in my speech. May what I have heard not leave me. I will speak what is right. I will speak what is true. May that protect me, and protect the one who speaks. Om, peace, peace, peace. This is satya, truthfulness, one of the oldest pillars of dharma: Patanjali lists it among the first restraints of yoga, right after not harming. And the chant gives it an exact shape. Truth is words and mind standing in the same place. Satyakama's words cost him; they matched his mind anyway. The tradition also argues about the other half of the line. The reciters keep every syllable of the Veda exactly, because the sound itself is held sacred. Yaska, an early teacher of what Vedic words mean, compares someone who recites without understanding to a post carrying a load. The chant holds both: exact words, rooted in the mind.
screen: `SPEECH ROOTED IN MIND.` · `SATYA: TRUTHFULNESS.` · `THE RECITERS: THE SOUND IS SACRED.` · `YASKA: A POST CARRYING A LOAD.` · then, large: `WORDS AND MIND IN ONE PLACE.`

segments.voice: The chant makes a promise: satyam vadishyami, I will speak what is true. If you pray, say those words softly, once or three times, the way the chant is said. If you don't, say it in English: I will speak what is true. Then choose one true sentence about today, short and plain, and say it out loud, slowly, meaning each word as it leaves you. Let the rest of the sit be quiet, words and mind standing in the same place.
The peace chants, and today van me manasi: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind in my speech.
Something to keep: satya, let your words match your mind. Satyakama's did. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Van me manasi is chanted as the peace chant of the Aitareya Upanishad; in traditional Vedic schools students learn recitation by ear, syllable by syllable, while commentators teach what the words mean.
